clips.narration: Welcome. Do not read the title. Introduce yourself, then the road map.

A European LTL, last-mile and warehousing carrier. It owns its fleet and drivers; it is not a broker. It moves different freight for different accounts at three service levels. What it sells is an on-time service level, backed by a credit of 1% of monthly spend per point missed, capped at 10%. Zurich is the non-EU leg and crosses customs.

Three tiles, three charts. Revenue up 4.55% to EUR 2,879,732. On time 93.28% against a 97% contract, down 3.95 points. EUR 52,955 in service credits, none in 2023-24. Shipments rose only about 3% a year, so 2025 is a reliability fall, not a volume story.

Left: Jaffle Werke, 33.5% of the book, slid from 86.1 to 78.7 on time through 2025 while the average of the other four stayed between 91.6 and 98.2; Werke's contract is 97%. Right: freight is 23.8% of shipments but 49.6% of the 135 misses, standard 55.9% of volume and 38.5% of misses, expedited 20.3% and 11.9%. Careful: freight is not hard in itself. 416 of freight's 479 shipments are Werke, and the other 63 never missed.

This is the second contributing factor in Jaffle Werke's 2025 on-time decline, beside the Paris storm (CRM review, 20 Oct). Vehicles and drivers are within ordinary variation, the maintenance record is ordinary, and it is the hub's own freight mix: the fleet is not the cause. It is a place. Bay 3 had no damage in 2023-24 and its staging dwell rose from about 46 to 70 minutes. Confidence is moderate, and the thing that would settle it is bay 3's equipment-inspection results. From Q4 on-time is tracked by cause and the hub runs an SOP audit; peak volume is kept off bay 3. Not measured: damage cost in euros. Damage rose at four of five hubs in 2025, so bay 3 is not the whole network's rise. The sources are messy: 14 of 15 incident reports name dock staging, and 5 reports cite IR-9003, 4 of them filed months before it existed, so free text needs provenance, not just retrieval. Full detail in the appendix.

For a decade the work product was an answer: a chart, a dashboard. Now it is the meaning, because that is what an agent reads, and an agent cannot ask a clarifying question. A dashboard answers once; meaning answers every question downstream of it. The models are the same. The audience is not. The job changes when the reader changes; the craft does not. And you are already most of the way there: you write meaning down for a living, you own the semantic layer, you already run the gate an agent needs (tests, contracts, freshness, lineage), and you write in the one language both readers share, versioned code.

Land on the offer, then stop talking. Repeat the three takeaways in one breath each, then the offer: Fivetran and dbt are here to help you get there faster, more efficiently, with built-in trust. Close by returning to the opening question: the hands that went up at the start are the people who now know how to fix it. Invite questions; the appendix has the working behind every number if someone wants to go deeper.
